Keeping Creativity Human: How AI and Art should coexist in Southeast Asia

By Kiera Wong, TFGI Insights Contributor

The Paradigm Shift: Unlike previous digital tools that changed how art is distributed or consumed, Generative AI (GenAI) disrupts the first stage of the UNESCO cultural cycle: original content creation.

The Core Tension: The commercial pressure to prioritise rapid, low-cost “products” threatens the time-consuming human “process” that serves as a vital vessel for Southeast Asia’s cultural memory.

The Way Forward: To prevent cultural dilution, SEA nations must implement robust Intellectual Property (IP) frameworks that protect human authorship, mobilise targeted funding, and foster a critical mindset shift that values the journey of creation over mere algorithmic output.

AI as the current (but not new) tech disruptor to the Arts

The rapid arrival of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has widely and rapidly impacted industries globally. While driving enhanced efficiency and innovation, AI disruption is also reshaping the future demand for professional skills, bringing into question the value of human input in an increasingly automated world.

In the creative industries, Generative AI (GenAI) triggers familiar anxieties about technological redundancies. Today, the average person can bypass skilled artists or creative professionals to create highly customised, visually aesthetic images. The anxiety of creatives’ redundancy is also paired with new ethical concerns of appropriating creative ideas and styles, as observed with the lawsuit over the trend of using ChatGPT to reproduce images in Studio Ghibli’s style which calls into question the importance of the human touch in creating art.

However, history has witnessed that the advancement of technology radically transforms the purpose, execution, and technique of the arts, rather than replacing them. From photography liberating the need for painting to computer graphics challenging traditional sketching, revolutionary technologies do not necessarily make industries redundant; they simply—and often painfully—restructure and re-evaluate the need for their existence.

In “Arts and Technologies in ASEAN: Interconnected Parts,” a qualitative study conducted by the British Council, SEA artists have long been adopting technology to produce works with meaningful human reflection—something that cannot be mimicked by automation alone. Beyond social media and GenAI, SEA artists have used, adapted, and advanced lighting, immersive technology, 3D technology, sensors, and sound production in order to push their narratives and expand their creative vocabularies.

How GenAI alters the Cultural Cycle

Yet, the disruption with GenAI is distinct and rightfully revolutionary. Referencing UNESCO’s Cultural Cycle as an analytical framework, the British Council outlines how tools like digital platforms and immersive technologies previously disrupted stages 02 to 05—that is, from production, to distribution, to delivery/transmission, to consumption/participation.

GenAI, however, is revolutionising innovations primarily at Stage 1: Content Creation—the very first step of the creative making process. Rather than simply assisting creative workflows or expanding distribution channels, GenAI is capable of generating original text, images, music or video, fundamentally redefining and challenging authorship and the role of human creator as we used to know. Artists from ASEAN have also begun adapting AI into other stages of the Cultural Cycle such as 05 Consumption/Participation.

How it has been disrupted by technology

Now, GenAI enables collaborative ideation, and artists in ASEAN have been integrating AI-generated ideas with cultural motifs (pg 37). For example, Mahkota Designs from Brunei Darussalam are able to use GenAI tools such as Midjourney and NewArc.ai to ideate for intricate and culturally inspired designs that reach a greater audience (pg 41).

A clear example of this occurred when Adobe raised its subscription prices, justifying the hike by pointing to the “value” of its new built-in AI features. For independent creators and smaller grassroots studios across Southeast Asia, such moves create steep financial dependencies. High fees and restrictive licensing models raise substantial barriers, forcing local creators to operate on tech giants’ terms rather than innovating freely on their own.

This combined pressure—to prioritise an efficient global “product” while being financially squeezed by proprietary tech platforms—hits Southeast Asia uniquely hard. In this region, the artistic process is rarely just about commercial labour; it functions as a vital vessel for collective memory and historical documentation.

How to safeguard Southeast Asian creativity and human authorship

Leaving the regional creative ecosystem to be shaped entirely by market forces and proprietary global monopolies guarantees a future of cultural erasure. To prevent this, Southeast Asia cannot afford to be a passive consumer of AI technology. Instead, the region requires a deliberate, structured intervention—one that legally safeguards human ingenuity, provides independent financial lifelines, and shifts the collective mindset to value the journey of creation as much as the final output.

IP is critical for creative technologies because it protects breakthroughs, encourages investment, and ensures artists receive monetary compensation for their original ideas. While some SEA countries already have stronger IP frameworks and are rewarded with more developed creative sectors, AI-related IP frameworks can further encourage human-led creativity.

NGOs can support socially valuable projects that may not attract commercial investment. Foundations such as the ASEAN Foundation can provide grants for creative projects employing technology that fosters cultural preservation, community storytelling, environmental art or to advocate for certain social causes. This is especially relevant where the project’s social/cultural value exceeds its commercial potential.

With corporations regularly seeking sponsorship and collaboration opportunities for social relevance, corporate sponsorships can provide resources and technology for larger-scale creative experimentation. For example, Google Arts & Culture and Jacquard’s artist residency brought artists together with Google engineers to develop interactive installations using Jacquard technology, demonstrating how corporate partnerships can provide artists with access to technological expertise and resources that enable new forms of creative expression.

It is natural for markets and startups to prize efficiency, but if we surrender our creative authorship to automation, we risk losing the very nuance that defines us. Stakeholders—from governments and educators to civil society—must step in to consciously protect and fund the human process. By building a resilient ecosystem that values the journey of creation as much as the final output, Southeast Asia can ensure its digital economy remains not just efficient, but deeply creative and culturally distinct.

Kiera Wong is a final-year Communications and New Media undergraduate at the National University of Singapore. Her interests lie at the intersection of technology, culture and society, particularly in how emerging technologies such as AI reshape creative industries and digital communities. She has experience across public affairs, policy communications, digital engagement and technology research, with a regional focus on Southeast Asia.

As a social entrepreneur, impact investor, and engineer, her experience spans over two decades in the MENA region, South East Asia, and Japan. She is founder of Woomentum, a Singapore-based platform dedicated to supporting women entrepreneurs in APAC through skill development and access to growth capital through strategic collaborations with corporate entities, investors and government partners.

Dr Ming Tan is Senior Fellow at the Tech for Good Institute; where she served as founding Executive Director of the non-profit focused on research and policy at the intersection of technology, society and the economy in Southeast Asia. She is concurrently a Senior Fellow at and the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore and Advisor to the Founder of the COMO Group, a Singaporean portfolio of lifestyle companies operating in 15 countries worldwide. Ming was previously Managing Director of IPOS International, part of the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore. Prior to joining the public sector, she was Head of Stewardship of the COMO Group.

Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics

Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (“AI“) shows no sign of slowing down, and with its increased proliferation, governments have been seeking to establish national frameworks to ensure the controlled and secure development and deployment of AI. In recognition of the cross-boundary nature of AI, governments have also been looking towards greater cooperation in AI framework building and standards equivalence.

In February 2024, the ASEAN member states issued the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (“ASEAN AI Guide 2024“), which establishes common principles and recommends best practices on the implementation of trustworthy AI in ASEAN. Standing as a landmark regional guide on AI policy, it seeks to help promote consumer confidence and facilitate cross-border deployment of AI services and solutions.

The ASEAN AI Guide 2024 has now been updated with the release of the Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics – Gen AI (“Gen AI Guide 2025“). The Gen AI Guide supplements and supports the ASEAN AI Guide 2024 with policy considerations related to Gen AI, highlighting the opportunities and risks of Gen AI, and recommending a range of policy actions for ASEAN to support its responsible adoption.

The issuance of the Gen AI Guide 2025 demonstrates the continually evolving nature of AI policy, which seeks to address developing technologies and manage emerging risks. It also shows the proactive approach that ASEAN member states are taking to facilitate a regional-level advancement in AI management.

This Update provides a summary of the key elements of the Gen AI Guide 2025, including the highlighted Gen AI risks and the policy recommendations.

The Gen AI Guide 2025 is designed as a resource for ASEAN policymakers to understand the primary challenges that they might encounter when working on subjects related to Gen AI, as well as potential strategies for addressing them.

The ASEAN AI Guide 2024 set out seven guiding principles for ensuring trust in AI and the design, development, and deployment of ethical AI systems. These principles continue to be relevant in the Gen AI Guide 2025 which highlights additional considerations in the context of Gen AI.

The guiding principles in the guides are as follows:

Transparency and Explainability

While the ASEAN AI Guide 2024 considers the risks posed by the adoption and development of traditional AI, the Gen AI Guide 2025 recognises that Gen AI may carry risks that are not typically associated with traditional AI, or risks that are enhanced and whose impacts or mitigations may change in the context of Gen AI. These risks, which include ethical, legal, and societal issues, require new approaches to governance.

The Gen AI Guide 2025 thus identifies the following unique Gen AI risks, which form the basis of its policy recommendations:

Mistakes and anthropomorphism: Gen AI systems can make highly coherent and persuasive mistakes, referred to as “hallucinations”.

Factually inaccurate responses and disinformation: Gen AI systems can amplify false or misleading information.

Deepfakes, impersonation, fraudulent and malicious activities: Gen AI systems pose risks of impersonation or misinformation by creating realistic content like deepfakes and phishing emails.

Infringement of intellectual property rights: Gen AI systems may lead to legal repercussions if copyrighted works are used as data to train the systems without an appropriate legal basis, or if the generated content too closely

The ASEAN AI Guide 2024 provides guidance on measures promoting the responsible use of AI that organisations should adopt. It also provides national-level recommendations to ensure responsible design, development, and deployment of AI systems, and regional-level recommendations for policy makers.

In contrast, the Gen AI Guide 2025 only sets out recommendations to regional policymakers at the ASEAN level. Recommendations to national policymakers are not included in this exercise.

Accountability: ASEAN can encourage and facilitate collaboration among developers, deployers, regulators, cloud providers, and civil society to create a common understanding on what shared responsibility would entail.

Data: ASEAN can work together to promote the collation of high-quality open datasets and support for industry data sharing. ASEAN can also develop a common approach towards the use and sharing of personal data across ASEAN, as well as data handling, storage, and governance for Gen AI.

Trusted Development and Deployment: ASEAN can explore establishing guidelines for the development and deployment of Gen AI models and/or applications, and should be aware of the critical need for upstream developers to share important information with their downstream deployers.

Incident Reporting: ASEAN can explore creating a common understanding around incident reporting and incident management.

Testing and Assurance: ASEAN can explore developing a regional benchmark that can facilitate testing to address concerns relevant to ASEAN (e.g. qualitative and quantitative indicators relevant to ASEAN’s unique linguistic, cultural, and societal contexts), as well as a list of evaluation tools and techniques preferred for use across the region.

Security: ASEAN can explore supporting and coordinating measures to promote vulnerability detection, promoting security knowledge-sharing among AI ecosystem stakeholders, and establishing guidelines on security by design.

Content Provenance: ASEAN can explore the adoption of content provenance technologies accompanied by policies and enforcement measures, as well as regional repository of real world examples of techniques and approaches towards establishing content provenance.

Safety and Alignment Research & Development: ASEAN can use its role to promote or convene platforms to facilitate the sharing of insights on AI safety and alignment research across member states and to help identify regional priorities for areas of further research.

AI for Public Good: ASEAN can create a regional compendium of responsible Gen AI use cases. It can also promote awareness and education on Gen AI, including skill development, digital literacy and risk awareness, and educational initiatives for workforces.

The Gen AI Guide 2025 seeks to highlight that the new challenges of Gen AI do not outweigh the substantial opportunities to improve lives, create economic opportunity, and empower new groups in society. It provides a policy-focused view of the risks and recommendations to promote responsible, risk-aware Gen AI use that ASEAN as a region should consider addressing. Importantly, the Gen AI Guide 2025 sets out the distinction between the risks and considerations between Gen AI and traditional AI, and delves deeper into the unique measures and approaches that are appropriate to Gen AI.

For further details, the ASEAN AI Guide 2024 is available here, and the Gen AI Guide 2025 is available here. Please feel free to contact our team for further queries.

These risks, which include ethical, legal, and societal issues, require new approaches to governance.
The Gen AI Guide 2025 thus identifies the following unique Gen AI risks, which form the basis of its policy recommendations:
Mistakes and anthropomorphism: Gen AI systems can make highly coherent and persuasive mistakes, referred to as “hallucinations”.
Factually inaccurate responses and disinformation: Gen AI systems can amplify false or misleading information.
Deepfakes, impersonation, fraudulent and malicious activities: Gen AI systems pose risks of impersonation or misinformation by creating realistic content like deepfakes and phishing emails.

Infringement of intellectual property rights: Gen AI systems may lead to legal repercussions if copyrighted works are used as data to train the systems without an appropriate legal basis, or if the generated content too closely

The ASEAN AI Guide 2024 provides guidance on measures promoting the responsible use of AI that organisations should adopt. It also provides national-level recommendations to ensure responsible design, development, and deployment of AI systems, and regional-level recommendations for policy makers.
In contrast, the Gen AI Guide 2025 only sets out recommendations to regional policymakers at the ASEAN level. Recommendations to national policymakers are not included in this exercise.

Accountability: ASEAN can encourage and facilitate collaboration among developers, deployers, regulators, cloud providers, and civil society to create a common understanding on what shared responsibility would entail.

Data: ASEAN can work together to promote the collation of high-quality open datasets and support for industry data sharing. ASEAN can also develop a common approach towards the use and sharing of personal data across ASEAN, as well as data handling, storage, and governance for Gen AI.

Trusted Development and Deployment: ASEAN can explore establishing guidelines for the development and deployment of Gen AI models and/or applications, and should be aware of the critical need for upstream developers to share important information with their downstream deployers.
Incident Reporting: ASEAN can explore creating a common understanding around incident reporting and incident management.

Testing and Assurance: ASEAN can explore developing a regional benchmark that can facilitate testing to address concerns relevant to ASEAN (e.g. qualitative and quantitative indicators relevant to ASEAN’s unique linguistic, cultural, and societal contexts), as well as a list of evaluation tools and techniques preferred for use across the region.

Security: ASEAN can explore supporting and coordinating measures to promote vulnerability detection, promoting security knowledge-sharing among AI ecosystem stakeholders, and establishing guidelines on security by design.

Content Provenance: ASEAN can explore the adoption of content provenance technologies accompanied by policies and enforcement measures, as well as regional repository of real world examples of techniques and approaches towards establishing content provenance.

Safety and Alignment Research & Development: ASEAN can use its role to promote or convene platforms to facilitate the sharing of insights on AI safety and alignment research across member states and to help identify regional priorities for areas of further research.

AI for Public Good: ASEAN can create a regional compendium of responsible Gen AI use cases. It can also promote awareness and education on Gen AI, including skill development, digital literacy and risk awareness, and educational initiatives for workforces.

The Gen AI Guide 2025 seeks to highlight that the new challenges of Gen AI do not outweigh the substantial opportunities to improve lives, create economic opportunity, and empower new groups in society. It provides a policy-focused view of the risks and recommendations to promote responsible, risk-aware Gen AI use that ASEAN as a region should consider addressing. Importantly, the Gen AI Guide 2025 sets out the distinction between the risks and considerations between Gen AI and traditional AI, and delves deeper into the unique measures and approaches that are appropriate to Gen AI.
For further details, the ASEAN AI Guide 2024 is available here, and the Gen AI Guide 2025 is available here. Please feel free to contact our team for further queries.

Some countries in the region are more mature in this field, and examining their current state can help understand how to harmonize approaches to strengthen capacity building, research, and catastrophic risk management. Shaped by its cultural diversity, political pluralism, and varied levels of development, Southeast Asia’s approach to AI safety governance combines localized, context-aware regulation with regional coordination, distilling lessons that could be applicable to other global majority regions. A woman walks past flags of ASEAN member nations. REUTERS/Adrees Latif (THAILAND) 3 min read Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky Print Conversations around AI safety are largely dominated by the United States, Europe, and China, leaving Southeast Asian voices underrepresented in broader global AI governance discourse. Still, countries in this region have made important strides in digital and AI policy, recognizing the opportunities presented by AI while adopting nuanced and pragmatic approaches to AI safety and development. This report, “AI Safety Governance, The Southeast Asian Way,” outlines recent AI governance developments in 11 Southeast Asian countries: Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam. Recommendations were in part developed through six roundtable discussions organized by AI Safety Asia (AISA), gathering insights from stakeholders ranging from government officials to the private sector, academia, and civil society. These conversations were used to identify regional priority areas for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and national governments over the next five years to develop comprehensive and future-proof approaches to AI safety. National governments can pursue pragmatic and impactful strategies while actively engaging with regional and international partners. To avoid friction between differing national strategies, ASEAN should harmonize approaches across the region and strengthen cooperation around capacity building, research, and risk management. The report also identifies several persistent challenges and gaps in AI policy across the region, such as developing national AI risk management plans. The Southeast Asian approach to AI governance also provides valuable lessons for other global majority countries crafting AI strategies. Given the incredible diversity of the region, Southeast Asian countries have taken a context-aware approach to AI policy, prioritizing open-source AI development, developing multilingual large language models (LLMs), and designing inclusive AI governance processes. Finally, this report serves as a call to action for countries in the region to address major gaps in policy, to usher in an inclusive, safe, and innovative AI future in Southeast Asia. cau.loi: Các bạn có biết các nước thành viên hiệp hội các quốc gia Đông Nam Á đã ban hành hướng dẫn của hiệp hội các quốc gia Đông Nam Á về quản trị và đạo đức trí tuệ nhân tạo nhằm thiết lập các nguyên tắc chung chưa?

cau.yDoHinh: Biểu đồ thể hiện sự tin cậy trong công nghệ.

cau.loi: Bên cạnh đó, theo nguồn tin chưa xác minh, tiếp cận quản trị an toàn trí tuệ nhân tạo tại Đông Nam Á kết hợp quy định mang tính địa phương, nhận thức ngữ cảnh với sự phối hợp khu vực để phản ánh sự đa dạng văn hóa và thể trị.
cau.chuTrenManHinh: Đa dạng văn hóa và thể trị
cau.yDoHinh: Bản đồ khu vực Đông Nam Á với các biểu tượng văn hóa.

cau.loi: Dựa trên các tài liệu chưa xác minh vừa nêu, chúng ta sẽ cùng nhau phân tích sâu hơn vấn đề này.
cau.yDoHinh: Biểu tượng sinh viên luật đang thảo luận nhóm.
